topic: Positions, organisational elements and ICS forms

notes.front: What is an Assistant, in ICS?
notes.back: A subordinate of a principal Command Staff position, with lesser capability and responsibility; may also be assigned to unit leaders.
notes.explanation: Assistant is the support title used specifically under Command Staff, distinct from Deputy, which supports command-level and section-level positions.
notes.example: Like a junior press officer helping the Public Information Officer manage a heavy media workload.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 71

notes.front: What is an Assisting Agency?
notes.back: An agency or organisation providing personnel, services, or other resources to the agency with direct responsibility for incident management.
notes.explanation: An assisting agency is actively helping deliver the response, unlike an agency that only offers indirect support.
notes.example: Like a neighbouring fire department sending engines to help fight a large blaze.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 71

notes.front: What is a Cooperating Agency?
notes.back: An agency supplying assistance other than direct operational or support functions or resources to the incident management effort.
notes.explanation: A cooperating agency helps, but not with the hands-on response work an assisting agency provides.
notes.example: Like a utility company sharing site maps, rather than sending crews into the field.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 72

notes.front: What is an Agency Representative?
notes.back: A person assigned from an assisting or cooperating agency, with authority to make decisions on that agency's participation in the incident.
notes.explanation: It is the specific person, not the agency itself, who can speak and decide on that agency's behalf at the incident.
notes.example: Like a company's authorised representative sent to a negotiation, empowered to agree terms on the spot.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 71

notes.front: What does the Operations Section Chief do?
notes.back: Is responsible to the IC for direct management of all operational activities; sets tactical objectives each operational period; helps prepare the IAP.
notes.explanation: The Operations Section usually holds the most resources and expands from the bottom up as the incident grows.
notes.example: Like a site foreman who runs the day-to-day work while reporting progress up to the project owner.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 16, SM-126

notes.front: What is a Staging Area?
notes.back: A temporary location for available resources in which personnel, supplies, and equipment await operational assignment.
notes.explanation: Only resources that are assigned and ready sit in a Staging Area; out-of-service resources do not belong there.
notes.example: Like a holding pen for players ready to be sent into a match at any moment.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 80

notes.front: What is a Division, in ICS?
notes.back: The organisational level responsible for operations within a defined geographic area.
notes.explanation: Divisions split an incident up by geography, so one supervisor is not stretched across an unmanageable area.
notes.example: Like splitting a flooded valley into an “upstream” team and a “downstream” team.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 73

notes.front: What is a Group, in ICS?
notes.back: An organisational subdivision established to divide the incident into functional areas of operation, not tied to one geographic area.
notes.explanation: Groups split an incident up by function instead of location, and can work across several Divisions at once.
notes.example: Like a water-rescue team that moves between both the upstream and downstream Divisions of a flood response.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 74

notes.front: What is a Branch, in ICS?
notes.back: A functional or geographic level between the Section Chief and Divisions/Groups in Operations, or between the Section and Units in Logistics.
notes.explanation: A Branch exists to keep the Operations or Logistics Section Chief's own span of control manageable.
notes.example: Like a regional division of a company, sitting between head office and the local branches.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 72

notes.front: What is the Air Operations Branch?
notes.back: A branch, on larger incidents, coordinating aviation resources for the Operations Section; it may split into an Air Tactical and an Air Support Group.
notes.explanation: On smaller incidents, aviation resources just report directly to the IC or the Operations Section Chief; a separate branch is only needed once aviation use grows.
notes.example: Like spinning off a dedicated air-traffic team once a project has enough flights to need one.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 22, SM-133

notes.front: What is a Task Force?
notes.back: Any combination of resources of different kinds and/or types, assembled for a mission, with common communications and a leader.
notes.explanation: A Task Force is defined by being mixed: different kinds or types of resource working together under one leader.
notes.example: Like a response team combining an ambulance, a fire engine and a police unit under one lead.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 81

notes.front: What is a Strike Team?
notes.back: A set number of resources of the same kind and type, with an established minimum number of personnel, common communications and a leader.
notes.explanation: Unlike a Task Force, every resource in a Strike Team is the same kind and type.
notes.example: Like five identical fire engines, each with the same crew size, working together under one leader.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 80

notes.front: What is a Resource Team?
notes.back: The law enforcement community's term for a Strike Team, added in NIMS 2017.
notes.explanation: It is the same concept as a Strike Team, just under a different name in law enforcement usage.
notes.example: Like calling the same vehicle a “lorry” in one country and a “truck” in another.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 79

notes.front: What is a Unit, in ICS?
notes.back: The organisational element with functional responsibility for a specific activity within the Planning, Logistics, and Finance/Administration Sections.
notes.explanation: Units are how those three Sections divide their own workload into named, manageable pieces.
notes.example: Like a company's payroll team being one small, named unit inside a larger finance department.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 81

notes.front: What is a Unit Leader?
notes.back: The individual in charge of a unit in ICS.
notes.explanation: Unit Leader is simply the standard supervisory title for whoever heads a Unit.
notes.example: Like a team lead responsible for one specific team within a department.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 81

notes.front: Who are Technical Specialists, and where do they first report?
notes.back: Advisors with special skills required at the incident, in any discipline; they initially report to the Planning Section and may be reassigned.
notes.explanation: A Technical Specialist can also cover a single Finance/Administration function on its own, without activating the whole section.
notes.example: Like bringing in a structural engineer for a building-collapse response, who might then be sent wherever their skill is needed.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 24, SM-135

notes.front: What does the Resources Unit do, within the Planning Section?
notes.back: It is responsible for all check-in activity and for maintaining the status of all personnel and equipment resources assigned to the incident.
notes.explanation: Everything the incident knows about who and what has checked in flows through this unit.
notes.example: Like a venue's guest-list desk, tracking exactly who has arrived and where they are.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 25 note, SM-137

image.alt: Expanded Planning Section chart showing the Planning Section Chief above four units - Resources, Situation, Documentation and Demobilization - plus Technical Specialists, who may report directly to the Section Chief.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from NIMS 2017, Fig. A-8, p. 101; IS-200.c SM, Lesson 4, Visual 25

notes.front: What does the Situation Unit do, within the Planning Section?
notes.back: It collects and processes information on the current situation, prepares situation displays and summaries, and develops maps and projections.
notes.explanation: Where the Resources Unit tracks people and equipment, the Situation Unit tracks the incident itself.
notes.example: Like a newsroom's live-updates desk, constantly building the current picture of events.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 25 note, SM-137

notes.front: What does the Demobilization Unit do, within the Planning Section?
notes.back: On large, complex incidents, it helps ensure an orderly, safe and cost-effective release of personnel once they are no longer needed.
notes.explanation: Sending resources home safely and efficiently is its own planning task, not something left to happen automatically.
notes.example: Like a stage crew planning how equipment and staff leave a venue once a show ends, not just how they arrive.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 25 note, SM-137

notes.front: What does the Documentation Unit do, within the Planning Section?
notes.back: It prepares the Incident Action Plan, maintains all incident-related documentation, and provides duplication services.
notes.explanation: It is the unit that turns the Planning Section's work into a physical, distributable plan.
notes.example: Like a project's records office, filing and copying every version of the plan as it changes.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 25 note, SM-137

notes.front: What units make up the Logistics Section's Service Branch?
notes.back: The Communications, Medical, and Food Units.
notes.explanation: Service Branch units keep responders connected, healthy and fed, so they can keep working.
notes.example: Like the “people-facing” services in a large event: radios, first aid, and catering.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 28, SM-140

image.alt: Logistics Section chart split into its Service Branch (Communications, Medical and Food Units, supporting responders directly) and Support Branch (Supply, Facilities and Ground Support Units, supplying and equipping the incident).
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from NIMS 2017, Fig. A-9, p. 104; IS-200.c SM, Lesson 4, Visuals 27-28

notes.front: What units make up the Logistics Section's Support Branch?
notes.back: The Supply, Facilities, and Ground Support Units.
notes.explanation: Support Branch units keep the incident equipped, housed and moving, as opposed to the Service Branch's people-facing units.
notes.example: Like the “logistics-facing” side of a large event: stock rooms, venue setup, and vehicle fleet.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 29, SM-141

notes.front: What does the Communications Unit do?
notes.back: Plans use of communications equipment and facilities; installs, tests, distributes and repairs equipment; supervises the Incident Communications Center.
notes.explanation: It handles the incident's radios and communications systems end to end, from planning through repair.
notes.example: Like an event's tech and radio desk, keeping every device working and charged.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 28, SM-139

notes.front: What does the Medical Unit do?
notes.back: Develops the Medical Plan and obtains medical aid and transport for injured or ill incident personnel, not the affected population.
notes.explanation: It exists to keep responders safe and cared for, distinct from any medical response to the public the incident is affecting.
notes.example: Like a workplace's own first-aid station, there to treat the staff, not the public passing by.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 27-28, SM-139

notes.front: What does the Food Unit do?
notes.back: Supplies food for responder personnel for the entire incident, including remote locations, and for people unable to leave their tactical assignments.
notes.explanation: It feeds the response workforce itself, wherever they are working, not the affected community.
notes.example: Like a catering team that follows a film crew to every location, not a soup kitchen for the public.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 28, SM-139

notes.front: What does the Supply Unit do?
notes.back: Orders personnel, equipment and supplies; receives and stores supplies; maintains an inventory; services nonexpendable equipment.
notes.explanation: Supply is the one Logistics function that supports the response beyond just its own personnel.
notes.example: Like a warehouse team ordering, storing and issuing stock for an entire operation.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 29, SM-141

notes.front: What does the Facilities Unit do?
notes.back: Sets up, maintains, and demobilises all facilities used in support of incident operations, and provides facility security.
notes.explanation: It handles the physical spaces the incident uses, from the Incident Command Post itself to camps.
notes.example: Like an events company setting up and later striking down a venue's tents and staging.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 29, SM-140

notes.front: What does the Ground Support Unit do?
notes.back: Supports out-of-service resources; transports personnel and supplies; fuels and maintains vehicles; implements the Traffic Plan.
notes.explanation: It keeps everything on wheels running and moving, including resources that are temporarily out of action.
notes.example: Like a race team's pit crew, keeping every vehicle fuelled, maintained, and able to get where it needs to go.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 29, SM-140

notes.front: What does the Time Unit do, within Finance/Administration?
notes.back: Records equipment and personnel time.
notes.explanation: It is the simplest of the four Finance/Administration units: pure time-recording.
notes.example: Like a timesheet office logging hours worked and equipment used.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 31, SM-143

notes.front: What does the Procurement Unit do?
notes.back: Administers all financial matters pertaining to vendor contracts, leases, and fiscal agreements.
notes.explanation: It handles the paperwork behind anything the incident buys or leases from outside vendors.
notes.example: Like a company's contracts desk, negotiating and administering agreements with outside suppliers.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 31, SM-143

notes.front: What does the Compensation/Claims Unit do?
notes.back: Handles financial concerns resulting from property damage, injuries, or fatalities at the incident.
notes.explanation: It deals with the financial fallout of harm the incident caused, not routine spending.
notes.example: Like an insurer's claims desk, processing payouts for damage and injury.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 31, SM-143

notes.front: What does the Cost Unit do?
notes.back: Tracks costs, analyses cost data, makes cost estimates, and recommends cost-saving measures.
notes.explanation: It is the unit that gives the incident a running picture of what the response is costing and how to spend more wisely.
notes.example: Like a project's finance controller, tracking spend and flagging where money could be saved.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 31, SM-143

notes.front: What are ICS Forms?
notes.back: Standard forms for recording and communicating key incident information in a format that is simple, consistent, and supports interoperability.
notes.explanation: For every form, know its purpose, who prepares it, and who receives it.
notes.example: Like a standard tax form: everyone fills in the same boxes, so anyone can read the result.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 35, SM-146

notes.front: What is ICS Form 201, Incident Briefing?
notes.back: An eight-part form giving the IC/UC status information for briefing incoming resources or a new IC: situation, objectives, current actions, and resource status.
notes.explanation: It is the first standard snapshot of the incident, usable before any more detailed planning documents exist.
notes.example: Like a handover note left for the next shift, covering what happened, what's planned, and who is where.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 36, SM-148

notes.front: What two kinds of decisions does the Incident Commander always approve?
notes.back: The Incident Action Plan, and all requests for ordering and releasing resources.
notes.explanation: Even once sections and staff are activated, these approvals stay with the IC.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 2, SM-110

notes.front: What is the only ICS requirement for using a Deputy?
notes.back: The Deputy must be fully qualified and equally capable of assuming the position.
notes.explanation: ICS places no restriction on a Deputy's home agency; only their qualification matters.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 4, SM-112

notes.front: When several agencies each send a Public Information Officer to an incident, what does the IC/UC do?
notes.back: Designates one as the lead PIO; all PIOs work in a unified manner, and the IC/UC approves the release of incident-related information.
notes.explanation: One voice, speaking consistently, is what keeps public messaging from contradicting itself across agencies.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Command Staff table, SM-117

notes.front: What are the rules for what belongs in a Staging Area, and who a Staging Area Manager reports to?
notes.back: Resources there are assigned and ready; out-of-service resources are not staged. The Staging Area Manager reports to the Operations Section Chief, or the IC.
notes.explanation: Keeping only ready resources in the Staging Area is what lets it be used at a moment's notice.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 17, SM-127

notes.front: When are branches established in Operations, how are they identified, and who manages them?
notes.back: When Divisions or Groups exceed the Operations Section Chief's span of control; identified by Roman numerals or a functional name; managed by a Branch Director.
notes.explanation: Branches are most often added for span of control, but they can also split work by function or area.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 20, SM-130

notes.front: What is one of the Planning Section's most important functions, beyond preparing the current plan?
notes.back: To look beyond the current and next operational period and anticipate potential problems or events.
notes.explanation: Planning is expected to think ahead of the response, not just document what is already happening.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 23, SM-134

notes.front: If an incident only needs one Finance/Administration function, such as cost analysis, must the whole section be activated?
notes.back: No. A Technical Specialist assigned to the Planning Section can provide that single function instead.
notes.explanation: ICS scales down as readily as it scales up: a whole section is never activated just to cover one small function.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 30, SM-141

notes.front: Where can the Intelligence/Investigations (I/I) function be placed within the incident command structure?
notes.back: In the Planning Section, the Operations Section, the Command Staff, a separate General Staff section, or some combination of these.
notes.explanation: I/I is a function, not a fixed box on the chart: the IC/UC places it wherever suits the incident.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 32, SM-144

notes.front: What are three important tools you should have available at an incident, according to the manual?
notes.back: The affected jurisdiction's Emergency Operations Plan; agency policies and procedures manuals; maps of the affected area.
notes.explanation: These tools give responders the context that ICS alone, as an organisational system, does not supply.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 34, SM-145

notes.front: What can ICS Form 201 occasionally serve as, before the Planning Section is established?
notes.back: The initial Incident Action Plan, until a Planning Section is established and generates one.
notes.explanation: This lets an incident have a working plan from the very start, even before any Section exists to write a full one.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 37, SM-149

notes.front: Besides ICS 201, what are a few other commonly used ICS forms, and what do they cover?
notes.back: For example: 202 Incident Objectives, 203 Organization Assignment List, 205 Radio Communications Plan, 214 Unit Log, 221 Demobilization Plan.
notes.explanation: A working responder is expected to know each form's purpose, who prepares it, and who receives it, not just that it exists.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 39, SM-152

notes.front: What are the three reasons to designate a Deputy Incident Commander?
notes.back: To perform tasks the IC requests; to take over in a relief capacity; and to represent an assisting agency that shares or may gain jurisdiction.
notes.explanation: A Deputy is not just a backup; they can also be a deliberate bridge to another agency.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 4, SM-112

notes.front: The Safety Officer is overwhelmed on a complex incident and is given a subordinate to help manage the workload, with lesser authority than the Safety Officer. What is that subordinate's title?
notes.back: Assistant.
notes.explanation: Assistant is the standard support title under a principal Command Staff position.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 71

notes.front: A neighbouring fire department sends engines and crews to work the fireline alongside the lead agency. What is that department, in ICS terms?
notes.back: An Assisting Agency.
notes.explanation: Assisting agencies provide the hands-on personnel, services or resources the response is using directly.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 71

notes.front: A utility company shares detailed site maps and technical advice with an incident, without sending crews to do fieldwork. What is that company's role?
notes.back: A Cooperating Agency.
notes.choices:
A) A Cooperating Agency
B) An Assisting Agency
C) An Agency Representative
notes.choicesExplained: B: assisting agencies provide direct operational or support resources, not just information. C: an Agency Representative is a specific person, not the agency's role in the response.
notes.explanation: Cooperating agencies help without taking on direct operational or support functions.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 72

notes.front: An assisting agency sends one named person to the incident, authorised to decide how that agency's resources are used. Who is this person?
notes.back: An Agency Representative.
notes.explanation: Their defining feature is the delegated authority to decide, not just to liaise informally.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 71

notes.front: An incident needs someone to set tactical objectives for the current operational period and manage all field activity, reporting to the IC. Who fills that role?
notes.back: The Operations Section Chief.
notes.choices:
A) The Operations Section Chief
B) The Planning Section Chief
C) The Incident Commander directly, always
notes.choicesExplained: B: Planning documents and prepares the plan, it does not directly manage tactical field activity. C: once an Operations Section is activated, its Chief manages this, not the IC personally.
notes.explanation: The Operations Section Chief exists specifically to take direct, day-to-day management of tactical operations off the IC's plate.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 16, SM-126

notes.front: Three engines are parked together, fuelled, crewed and ready, waiting for their next tactical assignment. Where are they?
notes.back: In a Staging Area.
notes.explanation: Everything in a Staging Area is assigned and ready to deploy, unlike out-of-service resources.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 80

notes.front: A flood response splits the affected valley into an “upstream” team and a “downstream” team, each managing everything happening in its own area. What organisational level is this?
notes.back: Divisions.
notes.explanation: Divisions split operations by geography.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 73

notes.front: A water-rescue team works across both the upstream and downstream Divisions of a flood response, handling one function wherever it is needed. What organisational level is this?
notes.back: A Group.
notes.explanation: Groups split operations by function, and can cross geographic boundaries that Divisions are bound by.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 19, SM-129

notes.front: The Operations Section Chief now has six Divisions and Groups reporting directly, exceeding a workable span of control. What level should be created?
notes.back: A Branch, to sit between the Operations Section Chief and the Divisions/Groups.
notes.explanation: Branches exist to restore a workable span of control once Divisions and Groups have grown too numerous to supervise directly.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 20, SM-130

notes.front: A response combines one ambulance, one fire engine and one police unit under a single leader for a specific mission. What is this grouping called?
notes.back: A Task Force.
notes.explanation: A Task Force is defined by mixing different kinds or types of resource under one leader; a Strike Team would be all the same kind and type.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 81

notes.front: Five identical fire engines, each with the same crew size, work together under one leader. What is this grouping called?
notes.back: A Strike Team.
notes.explanation: Every resource in a Strike Team is the same kind and type, unlike a Task Force's mixed resources.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 80

notes.front: A law enforcement agency refers to a Strike Team of identical patrol units using a different name. What is that name?
notes.back: A Resource Team.
notes.explanation: Resource Team is simply the law enforcement community's term for a Strike Team.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 79

notes.front: The Planning Section splits its workload into named teams, each responsible for one specific activity, such as tracking resources or documenting the plan. What organisational level is each of these?
notes.back: A Unit.
notes.explanation: Units are how Planning, Logistics and Finance/Administration divide their own responsibilities into manageable pieces.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, p. 81

notes.front: A structural engineer is brought onto an incident for their specialist knowledge and initially reports to the Planning Section. What ICS position is this?
notes.back: Technical Specialist.
notes.choices:
A) Technical Specialist
B) Unit Leader
C) Agency Representative
notes.choicesExplained: B: a Unit Leader heads a named unit; a specialist advisor is not automatically one. C: an Agency Representative acts for their agency's participation, not as a subject-matter advisor.
notes.explanation: Technical Specialists bring outside expertise and can be reassigned wherever the incident needs their discipline.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 24, SM-135

notes.front: An incident needs to know exactly which personnel and equipment have checked in and their current status. Which Planning unit provides that?
notes.back: The Resources Unit.
notes.explanation: Check-in activity and resource status are specifically the Resources Unit's responsibility.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 25 note, SM-137

notes.front: An incident needs a current map and summary of exactly what is happening right now. Which Planning unit provides that?
notes.back: The Situation Unit.
notes.explanation: Displays, summaries, maps and projections of the current situation are the Situation Unit's job.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 25 note, SM-137

notes.front: A large, complex incident is winding down and needs to release hundreds of personnel safely and efficiently. Which Planning unit helps with that?
notes.back: The Demobilization Unit.
notes.explanation: Sending resources home in an orderly, safe and cost-effective way is the Demobilization Unit's job.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 25 note, SM-137

notes.front: Someone needs the latest copy of the Incident Action Plan, and all records of the incident kept in order. Which Planning unit provides that?
notes.back: The Documentation Unit.
notes.explanation: It prepares the IAP itself and keeps the incident's full documentation and duplication services.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 25 note, SM-137

notes.front: An incident's radios, medical support for responders, and catering for the response workforce all sit under one Logistics branch. Which branch is this?
notes.back: The Service Branch.
notes.explanation: Communications, Medical and Food are the three units that make up the Service Branch.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 28, SM-140

notes.front: An incident's stock of supplies, its physical facilities, and its vehicle fleet all sit under one Logistics branch. Which branch is this?
notes.back: The Support Branch.
notes.explanation: Supply, Facilities and Ground Support are the three units that make up the Support Branch.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 29, SM-141

notes.front: A firefighter is injured while working the fireline and needs medical treatment and transport. Which Logistics unit arranges that?
notes.back: The Medical Unit.
notes.choices:
A) The Medical Unit
B) The Operations Section
C) The Food Unit
notes.choicesExplained: B: care for the affected population is managed under Operations, but care for an injured responder is the Medical Unit's role. C: the Food Unit only supplies food, not medical aid.
notes.explanation: The Medical Unit's job is medical aid and transport for incident personnel, not for the affected population.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 27-28, SM-139

notes.front: A responder needs new equipment ordered, received, and added to the incident's inventory. Which unit handles that?
notes.back: The Supply Unit.
notes.explanation: Ordering, receiving, storing and inventorying supplies is the Supply Unit's job.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 29, SM-141

notes.front: An incident needs an accurate record of how many hours each responder and each piece of equipment has been in use. Which Finance/Administration unit does that?
notes.back: The Time Unit.
notes.explanation: Recording equipment and personnel time is exactly the Time Unit's job.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 31, SM-143

notes.front: The incident needs to sign and manage a contract with an outside equipment vendor. Which Finance/Administration unit handles that?
notes.back: The Procurement Unit.
notes.explanation: Vendor contracts, leases, and fiscal agreements are administered by the Procurement Unit.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 31, SM-143

notes.front: A property owner files a claim for damage caused during the incident response. Which Finance/Administration unit handles that?
notes.back: The Compensation/Claims Unit.
notes.explanation: Financial concerns from property damage, injuries or fatalities go to the Compensation/Claims Unit.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 31, SM-143

notes.front: Command wants a running estimate of what the response is costing, plus suggestions for saving money. Which Finance/Administration unit provides that?
notes.back: The Cost Unit.
notes.explanation: Tracking costs, analysing cost data, and recommending savings is the Cost Unit's job.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 31, SM-143

notes.front: A new responder is handed an unfamiliar ICS form. What three things should they understand about it before using it?
notes.back: Its purpose, who is responsible for preparing it, and who needs to receive it.
notes.explanation: Every ICS form follows this same simple, consistent structure, which is what supports interoperability across agencies.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 35, SM-146

notes.front: An incoming Incident Commander needs a quick snapshot of the situation, current objectives, and resource status right at handover. What form gives them that?
notes.back: ICS Form 201, Incident Briefing.
notes.choices:
A) ICS Form 201, Incident Briefing
B) The Incident Action Plan
C) A Delegation of Authority
notes.choicesExplained: B: a full IAP may not exist yet at this point, which is why ICS 201 can stand in for it. C: a Delegation of Authority names who has command, it is not a situational briefing tool.
notes.explanation: ICS Form 201 is specifically built for briefing an incoming Incident Commander or team.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 36, SM-148

notes.front: The Logistics Section wants to release a resource that is no longer needed. Whose approval does that require?
notes.back: The Incident Commander's.
notes.explanation: The IC approves all requests for ordering and releasing resources, whichever section makes the request.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 2, SM-110

notes.front: An assisting agency that may gain jurisdiction later in the response wants direct visibility into command decisions. What is one way to accommodate that?
notes.back: Designate one of that agency's qualified people as a Deputy Incident Commander.
notes.choices:
A) Designate a Deputy from that agency
B) Give them an Agency Representative role only
C) Refuse, since only the IC's home agency can hold command roles
notes.choicesExplained: B: an Agency Representative can advise but does not sit inside the command structure the way a Deputy does. C: representing an agency that shares or may gain jurisdiction is one of the three stated reasons to use a Deputy.
notes.explanation: One of the three reasons ICS gives for a Deputy IC is exactly this: representing an agency that shares or may gain jurisdiction.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 4, SM-112

notes.front: An Incident Commander wants to appoint their most senior officer as Deputy, even though that officer has never trained on the position. Does ICS allow this?
notes.back: No. The only ICS requirement for a Deputy is that they be fully qualified and equally capable of assuming the position.
notes.explanation: Seniority is not the test for a Deputy; qualification for the position is.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 4, SM-112

notes.front: Three agencies at a joint incident each have their own Public Information Officer issuing separate statements. Does ICS doctrine support that?
notes.back: No: the IC/UC should designate one lead PIO, and all PIOs should work in a unified manner, speaking with one voice.
notes.explanation: Multiple, uncoordinated PIOs risk sending the public inconsistent messages.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Command Staff table, SM-117

notes.front: A broken-down engine, awaiting repair, is parked in the Staging Area alongside ready resources. Is that correct?
notes.back: No: out-of-service resources are not located in the Staging Area; only assigned, ready resources belong there.
notes.explanation: Mixing ready and out-of-service resources would undercut the whole point of a Staging Area: instant availability.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 17, SM-127

notes.front: Two Divisions are managing a wildfire's east and west flanks, each reporting directly to the Operations Section Chief. Can this stay as it is, or does it need a Branch?
notes.back: It can stay as it is: a Branch is only needed once the number of Divisions or Groups exceeds a manageable span of control.
notes.explanation: Branches are added as needed for span of control, not automatically whenever more than one Division exists.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 20, SM-130

notes.front: An incident's Intelligence/Investigations activity is light and closely tied to daily situation reports. Where might the IC/UC choose to place the I/I function?
notes.back: Within the Planning Section, for example, rather than as a separate General Staff section.
notes.explanation: I/I is placed based on the incident's needs; a lighter workload does not need its own General Staff section.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 32, SM-144

notes.front: An incident has no Planning Section yet, but the IC needs a working plan to brief the next shift. What form can stand in for the plan?
notes.back: ICS Form 201, which can occasionally serve as the initial Incident Action Plan until a Planning Section is established.
notes.explanation: This lets a response function even before the ICS organisation has fully grown into place.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 37, SM-149

notes.front: If the affected population, not just responders, needs medical care, which Section handles it?
notes.back: Operations, not the Medical Unit: Logistics functions (except Supply) support incident personnel, while care for the affected population is managed under Operations.
notes.explanation: The Medical Unit's scope is deliberately narrow, so it is never stretched to cover the wider public.
notes.contrast: Medical Unit = care for responders; Operations = care for the public the incident affects.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 27 note, SM-139

notes.front: What is the difference between a Division and a Group?
notes.back: Division: responsible for operations within a defined geographic area. Group: a functional subdivision, not tied to one geographic area.
notes.explanation: Divisions answer “where,” Groups answer “what function,” and a Group can work across several Divisions at once.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 19, SM-129

notes.front: What is the difference between a Strike Team and a Task Force?
notes.back: Strike Team: same kind and type of resource, with a set minimum number. Task Force: different kinds and/or types of resource, combined for a mission.
notes.explanation: Both have common communications and a single leader; the difference is whether the resources match or are mixed.
notes.source: National Incident Management System, Third Edition (October 2017), Glossary, pp. 80-81

notes.front: What is the difference between the Logistics Section's Service Branch and Support Branch?
notes.back: Service Branch: Communications, Medical and Food Units, all people-facing. Support Branch: Supply, Facilities and Ground Support Units, all materiel-facing.
notes.explanation: One keeps responders connected, healthy and fed; the other keeps the incident equipped, housed and moving.
notes.contrast: Service supports people directly; Support supplies things and places.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visuals 28-29, SM-139/141

notes.front: What is the difference between a Deputy and an Assistant in ICS?
notes.back: Deputy: fully qualified to take over command, a Section, or a branch. Assistant: a Command Staff subordinate, with lesser responsibility, not a stand-in for command.
notes.explanation: A Deputy can step fully into the role they support; an Assistant only helps carry its workload.
notes.contrast: Deputy can replace; Assistant only assists.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visuals 4 and 9, SM-112/119

notes.front: What is the difference between an Assisting Agency and a Cooperating Agency?
notes.back: Assisting agency: sends people or resources to the agency in charge. Cooperating agency: helps in other ways, without direct operational or support resources.
notes.explanation: Both sound like they are simply “helping”, but only an assisting agency provides personnel or resources to the agency running the response.
notes.contrast: Assisting agencies provide personnel or resources to the agency in charge; cooperating agencies help in other, non-operational ways.
notes.source: IS-0200.c Student Manual (September 2020), Lesson 4, Visual 12, SM-122
